paras: The threatened lynching of John Studebaker was a week-long mob threat in June 1888 against a farmer jailed at Jetmore, Hodgeman County, Kansas, for the shooting of his neighbor Thomas Andrews. A mob of more than 100 men was expected nightly, but the sheriff and armed townspeople guarded the jail, and no attack is reported.

Andrews lived about five miles west of Burdette in eastern Hodgeman County, and Studebaker lived across the road; the two had "something of a partnership" and had quarreled over two mules. According to the Wichita Eagle, on a Thursday Studebaker accused Andrews of stealing a post, and Andrews came out with a revolver, drew a line and dared him to cross it.

The next day, Friday, June 8, Studebaker was seen approaching Andrews's house with a double-barreled shotgun; two shots were fired, and Andrews, hit twice in the right breast, died a few hours later. Later that day Studebaker was reportedly found digging a grave for "the d——n rascal I have just killed" and was arrested. The Abilene Reflector reported "strong talk of lynching," while noting that he had "for some time been regarded as crazy."

By June 17 a Jetmore dispatch said that every night for more than a week a mob of over 100 men from the neighborhood of the killing had been expected in town, "determined on lynching Studebaker." Sheriff Gilland was said to be determined to protect the prisoner "at all hazards," and on the night of June 16 some 200 citizens met at the courthouse and pledged to stand by him. About forty men armed with Winchester rifles and shotguns guarded the jail that night, and the same number were to guard it the next.
The coverage ends with Studebaker still in jail; no report of a lynching, a trial or a ruling on his sanity was found.

The case ran briefly in Kansas and Nebraska papers between June 12 and June 18, 1888. The Wichita Eagle, in its column of state items, called it a "very singular murder" because "sufficient cause for such a deed is wanting," and closed with the friends' claim that Studebaker was insane. The Abilene Reflector's brief blamed "an old time feud" and mentioned the lynching talk in a single clause.

The Omaha Daily Bee gave the mob threat the most space, under the headline "OUTLAWRY IN KANSAS" with the deck "A Mob Looked For," and pairing it with a separate tarring and feathering of a Black man in the same county. Its dispatch praised the jail guards as "the best citizens," warned that "more blood would be shed before the trouble ends," and reported opinion divided between insanity and justification. None of the papers gave Studebaker's race.

The papers differ on motive: the Reflector named an old feud, the Eagle a quarrel over mules and a post that it judged insufficient cause, and the Jetmore dispatch reported some locals thought him insane while others claimed justification.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Studebaker
bases: A mob from the neighborhood of the killing was reported to be expected nightly at Jetmore 'determined on lynching Studebaker', and armed citizens guarded the jail against it; no attack is reported (A3, A4).

The threatened mob of 'over 100 men' would have acted without authority to punish Studebaker for the killing of Andrews, but no report shows that a mob reached the jail or that Studebaker was killed; the jail was guarded and the coverage ends with him in custody (A3, A4).

The killing of Andrews by Studebaker and his arrest are reported independently by the Wichita Eagle and the Abilene Reflector, and lynching talk by both the Reflector and a Jetmore dispatch in the Omaha Bee (A2, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Wichita Eagle (Kansas exchange item)
accounts.gist: A dispute over two mules led to quarrels; the day before the killing Andrews faced Studebaker with a revolver over a post; the next day Studebaker came with a shotgun and shot Andrews in his house, then was found digging a grave for 'the d——n rascal'.

accounts.label: Abilene Reflector state brief
accounts.gist: Studebaker went from his field to Andrews's home and shot him dead; there was strong talk of lynching though he had long been thought crazy; an old feud caused the crime.

accounts.label: Jetmore dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of over 100 had been expected nightly for more than a week; the sheriff and some 200 citizens pledged to protect the prisoner and armed men guarded the jail; opinion was divided between insanity and justification.

framing.detail: Kansas papers ran the killing as a 'very singular murder' for which 'sufficient cause ... is wanting', noting the claim of insanity, and mentioned lynching talk only in passing.
The Omaha Bee headlined the Jetmore dispatch 'OUTLAWRY IN KANSAS' and praised the 'best citizens' guarding the jail against 'mob violence'.

versions.value: An 'old time feud caused the crime'
Quarrels over two mules and a post between partners; yet 'sufficient cause for such a deed is wanting'
Insanity believed by some, justification claimed by others

conflicts.note: The accounts differ in emphasis rather than fact; the Wichita Eagle gives the most detail but relies on 'report' and 'an exchange'.

record_check.dossier: June 17 is the dispatch date; the killing was Friday, June 8, and the mob was expected nightly from about then; the citizens' meeting was the night of June 16.

record_check.record: said to have killed Thomas Andrews
record_check.dossier: Accused of shooting Andrews dead with a shotgun in Andrews's house after quarrels over mules and a post.
Not stated in any article; the 'negro' in the Omaha Bee dispatch is the victim of a separate tarring and feathering, not Studebaker.
Four white items in three papers, June 12-18, 1888.

info: Andrews was killed on a Friday ('last Friday' in a June 12 paper, i.e. June 8, 1888); the mob was expected nightly for more than a week up to the June 17 dispatch, and about 200 citizens met at the courthouse on the night of June 16.
Killing at Andrews's house about five miles west of Burdette, eastern Hodgeman County; threatened lynching at the jail in Jetmore, the county seat.
John Studebaker, a farmer near Jetmore (target of the threatened mob); race not stated.
Accused of shooting his neighbor Thomas Andrews dead in Andrews's house with a double-barreled shotgun after quarrels over two mules and a post.
A mob of men 'from the neighborhood of the killing', expected but not reported to have arrived.
Studebaker remained in jail as of June 17; no report of a lynching, trial or later outcome was found.
